To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) IVC filters are placed in patients with cancer more commonly than in patients without cancer; (2) IVC filters in cancer patients are placed more often in the setting of acute thrombosis and for prophylactic indications; (3) cancer patients are more likely to have IVC filter removal than patients without cancer; and (4) the risk of filter removal in cancer patients does not appear to be higher than that in patients without cancer.
the placement of an IVC filter in cancer patients with VTE was not associated with an improvement in the primary outcome of VTE-related mortality or with a decrease in the rate of recurrent VTE.
the IVC filter is not associated with a reduction of the risk of PE, and that the risk of complications associated with the IVC filter was higher in patients with malignancy.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of IVC filters in cancer patients is not supported by current literature and is not recommended.
the IVC filter should be used in cancer patients with VTE and high risk of PE and/or bleeding.

the use of inferior vena cava filters (IVCFs) in oncologic patients should be reserved for those patients who have a contraindication to anticoagulation and are not at risk for pulmonary embolism (PE) and that IVCFs should only be placed in the IVC and not the iliac vein.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
IVC filters are safe in cancer patients and that they are effective in preventing pulmonary embolism.

the inferior vena cava filters (IVCF) should be placed in patients who are high risk for developing a pulmonary embolism, have a contraindication to anticoagulation or are unable to receive anticoagulation.
we found that there is no clear indication to place IVC filter in cancer patients with a high risk of thrombosis, and that the indications should be the same as for the general population.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of IVC filters in the setting of acute DVT is not justified.
we need to be more thoughtful about the use of retrievable IVC filters in patients with cancer.
we should be placing filters in cancer patients with high bleeding risk and in patients with a high risk of thromboembolism.
